name: Kneeling or balance-ball chair

lead: Kneeling chairs and balance-ball chairs open the angle at the hips so the spine sits more upright and the lower-back curve is kept, instead of a slouched sit. The aim is a taller, straighter seated posture.

A sloped seat with shin rests tilts the pelvis forward, and a ball seat asks the body to make small balance adjustments. Small studies have measured lumbar curve, hip loading and muscle activity; they did not measure how people look.

paras: People use them for part of the workday, often alternating with a regular chair, since kneeling chairs are usually used intermittently. They are paired with standing breaks and posture exercises.
Studies report discomfort measures but no documented serious harms. Kneeling chairs load the shins and knees, and some users find long sessions tiring.

angle.text: Kneeling and balance-ball chairs open the hip angle so the spine sits more upright while you are seated on them. Small studies have measured lumbar curve and muscle activity.

lead: A kneeling chair supports the user with a sloped seat and padded shin rests so the thighs angle downward, opening the hip angle. A balance-ball chair uses an inflated exercise ball as the seat. Both are marketed as active seating that encourages upright posture.[1]

Grokipedia dates the modern kneeling chair to Norway in the late 1970s, with Hans Christian Mengshoel's Balans and Peter Opsvik's Variable chairs.[1] Studies measured lumbar curvature, hip loading and muscle activity in kneeling configurations, with small samples.[2][3][4][5]

paras: A kneeling chair has a forward-tilted seat, shin rests and often a rocker base. Height adjustment commonly uses a gas lift.[1]

A modelling study of a virtual male population estimated hip joint reaction force and hip flexion angle for a simple chair, car seat and kneeling chair, reporting a lower force in the kneeling configuration.[2] A comparison asked whether ergonomic kneeling chairs preserve lumbar curvature better than a standard computer chair.[3] A pilot study of 10 patients with chronic low back pain and 10 matched controls measured pelvic and lumbar parameters on radiographs.[4] A radiographic study of 20 asymptomatic subjects compared standing with seated variants.[5] A 2026 study assessed four kneeling chair angle combinations for muscle activity and perceived discomfort.[6] No studies found of balance-ball chairs in the sources consulted, and none test either chair for appearance.

timeline.event: Modern kneeling chair developed in Norway, per Grokipedia.[1]
